lead: A dual converter is two fully controlled rectifier bridges connected back to back to the same load. One bridge, converter P, can pass current in the forward direction; the other, converter N, can pass current in the reverse direction. By setting the firing angles correctly, the load can get positive or negative voltage and current, so the drive works in all four quadrants. This is used where a DC motor must reverse quickly, such as a rolling mill or a crane. The two bridges must either take turns or share through a reactor that limits circulating current.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for the fully controlled bridge and Unit 1 for commutation.

blocks.text: A dual converter is built from two fully controlled rectifier bridges joined at their DC terminals. Converter P is the positive-current bridge. Converter N is the negative-current bridge. Each bridge can set its own average DC voltage by its firing delay. For a single-phase bridge with continuous current, the average is V1 = (2Vm/π) cos α1. Vm is the peak supply voltage in volts; α1 is the firing delay of converter P in degrees; V1 is the average DC voltage of converter P in volts. Converter N uses α2 = 180° − α1, so V2 = (2Vm/π) cos α2 = −V1. This is the ideal balance. It makes the two open-circuit averages equal in size and opposite in sign, so no steady DC voltage is forced across the reactor that links them. The load can receive positive or negative voltage, and current can flow from P or from N. That gives four-quadrant operation: voltage and current can each be positive or negative.

Non-circulating mode lets only one bridge conduct at a time. While converter P supplies the load, converter N gets no gate pulses. At reversal, P is blocked, both bridges wait for a short dead time, then N is released with α2 = 180° − α1. The dead time lets the thyristors of P turn off and recover before N fires. The cost is a short interval with no torque.

Circulating-current mode keeps both bridges enabled. Their average voltages are set to match, but their instantaneous voltages are not equal because each bridge has ripple. That ripple drives a current around the loop formed by P and N. An intergroup reactor, an inductor placed between the two bridges, limits this circulating current. The reactor carries the ripple current without saturating and keeps the loop current within the thyristor rating. The load current is the difference between the two bridge currents.

A real dual converter must either block the circulating path or limit it. If both bridges conduct with no reactor, the supply sees a low-impedance thyristor path and a large current can flow even when the average voltages cancel. Non-circulating mode blocks by gating; circulating mode limits by inductance.

sections.h3: Where the dual converter is used

blocks.text: Reversible rolling-mill drives need forward torque to bite into the metal and reverse torque to brake or back the rolls out. A crane hoist needs torque in the lifting direction to lift a load and to hold it, and torque in the opposite direction to lower a light load under power; an overhauling load is lowered regeneratively with the lifting-direction current. Either way the drive must supply both current directions. In these drives the motor may have to produce torque in either direction while the speed stays positive, or brake while speed is negative. A single bridge cannot reverse current. A dual converter does it without reversing contactors, because converter P and converter N give the two current directions. Some syllabi call this a four-quadrant converter. The price is extra thyristors, a reactor or dead-time control, and more complex firing logic. Small drives often use a single bridge with a reversing contactor instead; dual converters appear where fast, frequent reversal is worth the cost. The same arrangement is used in reversible DC test benches and some high-power supplies.

spec.title: Dual converter example
spec.aria: Two converters joined at a common load, one controlling forward current and the other reverse current, both fed from the same AC supply.

examples.question: A dual converter feeds a 5 Ω resistor in series with a large inductor, so the load current is continuous, from a 230 V, 50 Hz single-phase supply. Converter P is fired at α1 = 30°. (a) Find V1 and the load current I. (b) Find α2 needed for converter N so its average voltage matches V1 in magnitude and opposite in sign, and state V2.
steps: Peak supply voltage: Vm = √2 × 230 V = 325.3 V.
Bridge voltage scale: 2Vm/π = 2 × 325.3 V / π = 207.1 V.
The large series inductor keeps the current continuous, so the continuous-current formula V1 = (2Vm/π) cos α1 applies.
Converter P average: V1 = 207.1 V × cos 30° = 207.1 V × 0.8660 = 179.3 V.
Load current: I = V1 / R = 179.3 V / 5 Ω = 35.9 A.
examples.check:
import math
Vm = 230 * math.sqrt(2)
base = 2 * Vm / math.pi
V1 = base * math.cos(math.radians(30))
I = V1 / 5
alpha2 = 180 - 30
V2 = base * math.cos(math.radians(alpha2))
print(round(V1, 1))
print(round(I, 1))
print(round(alpha2))
print(round(V2, 1))

traps: Do not set α2 = α1. The complementary bridge needs α2 = 180° − α1; equal angles do not make the two average voltages cancel.
Do not say both bridges conduct in non-circulating mode. Only the selected bridge gets gate pulses; the other is held off even though its thyristors may see supply voltage.
Matching average voltages does not remove circulating current in circulating-current mode. Ripple makes the instantaneous voltages differ, so the intergroup reactor is still needed.
Watch the sign of V2. For α1 < 90°, α2 = 180° − α1 > 90°, so cos α2 is negative and V2 is negative.
Use degrees consistently. A calculator left in radian mode gives a wrong cosine for 30°.

quiz.q: State the ideal firing-angle relation for the two bridges of a dual converter.
quiz.a: α2 = 180° − α1, so V2 = −V1 when the bridges are identical.

quiz.q: Why is a dead time needed when a non-circulating dual converter reverses?
quiz.a: To let the outgoing bridge's thyristors turn off and recover before the incoming bridge fires, preventing a direct path from one bridge to the other.

quiz.q: A single-phase dual converter has Vm = 325 V. Converter P is fired at α1 = 60°. Find V1 and the matching α2.
In circulating-current mode the average voltages are equal. Why does current still circulate, and what limits it?
quiz.a: The instantaneous bridge voltages have ripple, so a ripple voltage drives current around the P-N loop. The intergroup reactor's inductance limits the current.

quiz.q: In non-circulating mode converter P supplies 35.9 A. What is the current through converter N?
quiz.a: 0 A, because N is gated off and no current path is provided.

quiz.q: How does a dual converter give four-quadrant operation?
quiz.a: Converter P can supply positive current and converter N negative current; each bridge can also set positive or negative average voltage by its firing angle. Thus V and I can each have either sign.

quiz.q: What is the danger if the intergroup reactor saturates in circulating-current mode?
quiz.a: Its inductance falls, so the ripple-driven circulating current rises sharply. The thyristors and reactor can be overstressed; the reactor must be designed not to saturate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial DC drives still use dual converters where very fast torque reversal is needed, but AC drives with field-oriented control have taken much of that market. In HVDC and large industrial rectifiers, related twelve-pulse and back-to-back bridge arrangements appear, though the control aims differ. Newer curricula connect the dual converter to four-quadrant drive models and to grid-connected converter control. Search next for “four-quadrant DC drive”, “circulating current dual converter”, and “intergroup reactor”.
